title: The Sleeping Choir
premise: Wendell Reyes takes a teaching post at Hollow Creek Elementary, where a class of students vanished decades ago and the town's oldest house—the one his grandmother left him—keeps adding an empty chair to every family photograph. As he documents the school's strange absences, he discovers the missing class was 'signed in' by the house's previous resident as a choir for something that sleeps beneath it, and that his inheritance makes him next in line to sign. To free the children and himself, Wendell must hold out until sunrise inside the house, refuse to sign, and sing the counter-song the vanished teacher left hidden in her lesson plans—breaking the contract before dawn.
about_author: Isandro Joubert is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent eleven years in small-town classrooms before turning to horror full-time. They write about institutions, inheritance, and the quiet violence of belonging somewhere you were never meant to stay.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: Wendell Reyes arrives in Hollow Creek to teach fifth grade, photographing every classroom wall because documentation steadies him. His students are polite but count themselves aloud each morning, always arriving at twenty-four even when children are visibly absent. POV: Wendell. Beat: uneasy wonder—the town feels welcoming in a way that feels rehearsed.

chapters.title: The Twenty-Fourth Desk
chapters.summary: Wendell finds a desk in his classroom that no roster accounts for, its surface carved with initials from 1971. The custodian, Marisol, warns him never to move it. That night his classroom roster prints itself with a name smudged beyond reading. POV: Wendell. Beat: first crack in normalcy; curiosity curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House
chapters.summary: Wendell moves into the house his grandmother left him on the edge of town. Neighbors cross the street rather than pass it. He unpacks boxes of old family photographs and notices, in the background of a 1980s snapshot, a wooden chair that doesn't belong to any room he knows. POV: Wendell. Beat: grief braided with creeping wrongness.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Comparing photographs across decades, Wendell confirms the chair appears in every image taken at the house—and it is closer to the camera in each successive decade. His documentation instinct kicks in: he builds a timeline. Marisol sees the photos and goes pale, refusing to explain. POV: Wendell. Beat: obsessive dread; the past assembling into a pattern.

chapters.title: The Missing Class of '71
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Wendell finds that an entire fifth-grade class disappeared in October 1971; the official record lists them as relocated. Their teacher, Adeline Voss, resigned the same week and was never seen again. The principal urges him to stop asking. POV: Wendell. Beat: institutional stonewalling; power protecting itself.

chapters.title: Counting Aloud
chapters.summary: During a fire drill, Wendell counts his students and gets twenty-five—then recounts and gets twenty-four, though no child has left the line. One student, Imani, whispers that 'the extra one only comes when you look.' Wendell starts sleeping with the lights on. POV: Wendell. Beat: fear made intimate; the supernatural touching his daily care for his students.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Marisol finally talks: her aunt was in the Class of '71. Adeline Voss didn't take them—they were taken by the thing under the Reyes house, invited by the then-owner, Elias Reyes, Wendell's great-grandfather, who signed papers promising 'voices for the sleeper.' Marisol begs him to sell the house. POV: mostly Marisol via her account, framed by Wendell. Beat: revelation; the horror has Wendell's own name on it.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: Searching the attic, Wendell finds a leather folio: a contract in Elias's hand, renewed by his grandmother, due for renewal by 'the last resident'—him. The signature line is warm to the touch. That night, every photograph in the house shows the chair pulled up to an empty place set at his table. POV: Wendell. Beat: trap closing; inheritance as predation.

chapters.title: Adeline's Lesson Plans
chapters.summary: In a locked school storage room, Wendell finds Adeline Voss's surviving lesson plans, annotated in margins with musical notation—a song she called 'the counter-choir,' meant to unmake what was sung in. Pages are missing, torn out deliberately. POV: Wendell. Beat: hope with teeth; a weapon exists but is incomplete.

chapters.title: Imani Knows the Words
chapters.summary: Imani, whose great-aunt was also among the vanished, has hummed fragments of the notation all her life without knowing why. She and Wendell compare her remembered melody to Adeline's pages; they fit like puzzle pieces. Together they decide to finish the song. POV: alternating Wendell and Imani. Beat: found family forming—teacher and student as co-conspirators.

chapters.title: The House Sings Back
chapters.summary: As their work progresses, the house retaliates: doors rearrange, the chair appears physically in Wendell's kitchen, and recordings of his voice play back with extra voices underneath. His documentation—photos, tapes—becomes evidence of haunting and, worse, of invitation. POV: Wendell. Beat: escalation; the house is aware and offended.

chapters.title: The Town That Signed
chapters.summary: Wendell confronts the town council, discovering half the founding families' names appear as witnesses on copies of the contract across generations. The prosperity of Hollow Creek was purchased with the choir. The mayor offers him money to sign quietly. POV: Wendell. Beat: theme crystallized—power corrupted into complicity; the whole town is an accomplice.

chapters.title: Twenty-Four Empty Seats
chapters.summary: On the anniversary night, all of Wendell's students dream the same dream and arrive at school hollow-eyed, humming a hymn none of them learned. The sleeper beneath the house is tuning itself to new voices. Imani's humming turns involuntary. POV: Imani. Beat: stakes become personal and bodily; the children are being harvested.

chapters.title: The Missing Pages
chapters.summary: Following Adeline's marginalia, Wendell locates her last known address—an abandoned farmhouse where he finds the torn pages sealed in a wall, along with her final journal entry: she went into the house to sing alone and failed because she had no one to hold the door. POV: Wendell. Beat: tragic predecessor; the cost of trying this alone.

chapters.title: Assembly
chapters.summary: Wendell recruits allies: Marisol, Imani, and two students whose families never signed. They plan to enter the house at midnight and hold out until sunrise while Wendell sings the completed counter-song. Each ally takes a role—door, light, witness. POV: Wendell. Beat: resolve; found family weaponized against inherited evil.

chapters.title: Midnight, First Hour
chapters.summary: They enter at midnight. The house unfolds inward, rooms repeating, the dining table set for twenty-four with the chair at its head. Wendell begins the song; the walls answer in the voices of children. Marisol holds the front door open against pressure like deep water. POV: Wendell. Beat: descent; awe and terror entwined.

chapters.title: The Choir Appears
chapters.summary: The Class of '71 manifests—still ten years old, mouths moving in the sleeper's hymn. Wendell recognizes his grandmother's brother among them. The song falters when he sees the faces; the house surges, extinguishing their lights one by one. POV: Marisol. Beat: heartbreak; the enemy wears beloved faces.

chapters.title: The Signature Line
chapters.summary: The house offers Wendell the folio and a pen: sign, and the children return, his grandmother included—in service. It shows him visions of belonging, of being needed, of a town that would finally love him. Imani grips his hand and keeps humming. POV: Wendell. Beat: climax of temptation; power and belonging offered as one poisoned gift.

chapters.title: Counter-Song
chapters.summary: Refusing to sign, Wendell sings the finished counter-song with Imani harmonizing—the living voice answering the stolen ones. The Class of '71 falters, then joins, their own voices breaking the sleeper's hymn apart. The house screams through every room. The chair splinters. POV: alternating Wendell and Imani. Beat: climax; collective voice defeating solitary power.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Dawn floods the ruined dining room. The Class of '71 ages decades in seconds and fades with gratitude, Adeline Voss last, mouthing thank you. The contract crumbles to ash. The house stands ordinary and cold, its extra rooms gone. Marisol closes the door behind them. POV: Wendell. Beat: release; grief and victory inseparable.

chapters.title: Recounting
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Wendell's class counts twenty-three—one child moved away, truly gone this time, mourned honestly. The town council resigns amid the exposed records; some neighbors thank him, others shun him. Imani gives him a drawing of twenty-four chairs, one broken, labeled 'theirs.' POV: Imani. Beat: aftermath; truth as costly repair.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Wendell boxes his photographs to send to the families of the lost, keeping only one: the earliest image, where the chair is farthest away and almost invisible. On the back, in his grandmother's hand: 'Remember them louder than they were taken.' He teaches on. POV: Wendell. Beat: resolution; memory as vigilance, belonging chosen rather than signed for.
